questions.q: What was the actual root cause of Failure 1, where Salesforce saves hung during the ERP's seasonal slowdown?
options: Salesforce itself had a bug unrelated to any integration
A synchronous, blocking callout was placed on the critical path of a common user action, so a slow ERP response held open Salesforce transaction threads under load
The ERP was completely offline with no response at all
The sales surge exceeded Salesforce's total storage limit
questions.explain: The symptom (hanging saves) traced back to a synchronous callout on the Opportunity-close path -- once the ERP slowed down, that blocking dependency backed up transaction threads for every rep trying to close a deal.

questions.q: What caused the duplicate customer records described in Failure 2?
options: A sync matched records by customer name instead of a dedicated External ID, so a difference in name capitalization caused the sync to create a second record instead of updating the existing one
The ERP does not support External ID fields at all
Salesforce automatically duplicates every Account record every 24 hours
The Bulk API has a known bug that creates duplicate rows
questions.explain: Matching on a human-entered, non-stable field like name meant a simple casing difference caused the sync to treat the same real customer as two different records.

questions.q: What is the recommended structural fix for Failure 2, beyond a one-time cleanup?
options: Manually merge duplicate records every week going forward
Backfill a proper External ID on both sides using each system's stable key, and remove the name-based matching path so it can't recreate the problem
Disable the ERP sync permanently
Rename every Account in Salesforce to match the ERP exactly, one time only
questions.explain: A one-time merge only fixes the existing duplicates; the structural fix removes the matching logic that caused the duplication in the first place, so the same mistake can't recur.

questions.q: What specifically caused the sync loop in Failure 3?
options: Both directions of a bidirectional sync fired on 'record changed' with no mechanism to recognize and skip a change that originated from the other side of the sync itself
The ERP and Salesforce were running on incompatible API versions
A single sync job was scheduled to run twice per day instead of once
The Account object had no Last Modified field
questions.explain: Without loop prevention, each side's sync-triggered update looked indistinguishable from a genuine user change, so each update re-triggered the opposite-direction sync endlessly.

questions.q: What kind of mechanism does this lesson describe as the well-known fix for a bidirectional sync loop?
options: Tagging sync-originated updates (e.g., a flag or a dedicated integration user) so each side can recognize and skip a change it only just caused itself
Running both directions of the sync less frequently so the loop takes longer to notice
Disabling one direction of the sync permanently with no replacement
Increasing the Apex callout limit to accommodate the extra sync traffic
questions.explain: Loop prevention works by letting each side distinguish 'a change a real user made' from 'a change my own sync just caused,' so it can skip re-propagating the latter.
